plannedVideo: Why did scientists build a floating laboratory that tipped 90 degrees into the ocean?
coldViewerPull: A floating structure normally stays upright by avoiding a huge tip. Here scientists designed the tip; the viewer wants to know why anyone would work inside it and how it stays afloat.
expectedPayoff: The bizarre orientation was the tool: to measure the moving ocean, scientists needed their measuring platform to move much less with it. It remained floating; the huge submerged hull explains why it was more than a tipping trick.

truthEvidenceStatus.framing: Historic FLIP was a floating research platform towed horizontally and intentionally tipped into vertical operation. Preliminary former-operator documentation supports its use as a stable measurement platform with most of its length submerged and reduced wave response. Established central design, not final verification of each explanatory model, timing or numerical claim.
caveats: A spar buoy/research platform, not an ordinary self-propelled ship; never claim it sank, became perfectly still or defeated every sea condition.
Detailed explanation of waterplane geometry, buoyancy distribution and ballast sequence needs primary engineering review. Source supports reduced response, not a universal animated physical model.
Historic 10m wave / <1m vertical motion observation is conditional; omit unless conditions/provenance adequately checked.
Scripps pages share institution; DEEP marketing partly derives from Scripps. Source count is not independent replication.
Refurbishment/relaunch is current and incomplete in inspected sources; keep historical treatment, no present operational claim.
Original illustrative geometry is feasible; external photos/video require separate rights review after approval.

intendedStory: Establish the deliberate tip; reveal that researchers needed a steady measurement reference; follow controlled ballast change into vertical floating geometry; reveal the much longer hull below the surface and its reduced wave response; resolve with above-water laboratory and deep instruments sharing a steadier reference. Optional interior orientation detail only if it aids the same question.
whySelected: Selected on independent merit: headline invites why and how, and the first answer (ballast rotates it) opens the stronger answer (a moving instrument can confound ocean measurements). One object supports spatially connected understanding. Frigatebirds match its wonder and have stronger direct experimental access; their aerodynamic-control/low-sleep explanation is partly unresolved. Rai has excellent social insight but the honest stationary-transfer question loses the spectacular sunken-money hook. Manuscript evacuation has greater human stakes; its current evidence supports aggregate logistics more than a safely detailed individual story. FLIP wins even if all had equal source access; engineering views and rendering familiarity earn no advantage.
materialRisks: A simplified wave/buoyancy explanation can become false if reduced response is portrayed as total immunity. Detailed engineering evidence and visual truth review are mandatory after approval.
If the complete physical explanation cannot be made intelligible without a material premise/payoff change, return to discovery/Premise Review rather than rescue with spectacle.
decision: APPROVE PREMISE, REJECT PREMISE with reason, or REVISE PREMISE / FRAMING with specific feedback. Approval permits further research/development only; no claims, script, master or release approved.
